title: Where are our programs actually running?
learnerCopy:
We have spent the first four lessons looking inside a computer. We know how a process obtains memory, how the CPU executes instructions, and how a conventional TCP connection moves bytes between processes. We have also seen how an RDMA provider prepares memory and communication resources.

Now we will follow two real Python programs through a complete transfer. We are not going to write a new program in the browser. Instead, we will examine an experiment that FabricLab has already run on two Linux virtual machines.

On Server A (`hosta`), the Python process plays the sender. On Server B (`hostb`), another Python process plays the receiver. Both execute the same file, `exp_b_send_recv.py`, with different role arguments. They use Pyverbs to request RDMA operations through the Linux RDMA stack. Their RDMA device is the software device `rxe0`, associated with the data Ethernet interface. Remember: RXE executes the RDMA transport in software. A physical RNIC can implement much of this transport in hardware, but this experiment does not measure hardware offload.

There are two conversations between the machines. The control connection uses ordinary TCP on the control network. The programs use it to tell each other which RDMA endpoints they created and when they are ready. The data network carries actual RoCEv2 traffic. These are separate interfaces in our laboratory, not a universal requirement for RDMA.

We will follow the source code, instructions, packets and memory observations. The browser lets us reveal the recorded execution at our own pace. An illustrated queue transition is our explanation of the mechanism; a packet or application log is what was actually recorded.
visualSpec: Initial two-host bench, with visible A sender and B receiver, one CPU/RAM and provider/interface per host. Two separately labelled network links using `hosts.hosta/hostb.controlIp/dataIp`: TCP control and RoCEv2 data. Show actual device `rxe0`, associated `data0` interface, and guest Linux information from `environment`. Action **Inspect the two programs** reveals actual argument/role source lines `exp_b_send_recv.py:76–99` and an expandable link to the complete snapshot; no invented shell prompt. Action **Locate the capture** highlights the data path and links `send-recv.captureDownload.path`; no claim that TCP control was captured. Primary progression **Prepare the endpoints**.
revealCopy: The control path prepares the experiment. The data path carries the RDMA message. Both use Ethernet/IP in this lab, but the control messages travel through a conventional TCP socket and the RDMA operations use a different transport and programming interface.

title: What does a prepared connection actually contain?
learnerCopy:
Before either program can transfer a message, it needs a local RDMA device context, a protection domain (PD), a completion queue (CQ), a buffer associated with a memory region (MR), and a queue pair (QP). These are the objects we learned to build in the previous lesson.

Look at the actual setup code. It opens the device and identifies a local GID, creates a PD and CQ, then calls a helper that allocates a buffer, registers it and creates a QP. The CQ is separate from the QP; this particular helper associates one CQ with both the send and receive queues. The two queues can hold multiple requests. Here we use only one send and one receive.

A newly created QP is not ready to perform this transfer. Each process needs information about its peer. In this program the processes exchange a QPN, initial packet sequence number (PSN) and GID over TCP. The GID is a network identity used by the RDMA addressing machinery; in this lab it represents an IPv4-mapped address. It is not the QPN or an RKEY.

The helper configures the QPs in stages. In INIT it sets local port and access attributes. In RTR (Ready to Receive) it sets peer addressing, peer QPN and the expected incoming packet sequence. In RTS (Ready to Send) it sets outgoing sequence and retry attributes. These are local configuration actions, not a TCP three-way handshake. The lab takes both QPs through RTS before posting the SEND operation.

The numbers here belong to this SEND experiment. The QPNs we saw in the resource-only experiment belonged to a different run. A number that appears in two runs is not a guarantee that it identifies the same object.
visualSpec: Progressive actual setup ledger: **Open device and create resources**, **Exchange endpoint metadata**, **Prepare the QPs**. Show source `exp_b_send_recv.py:50–72,88–99`, `rdma_common.py:131–151,155–191`. Show per-host actual MR/PD/CQ/QP associations from `send-recv` evidence; use `endpoints`, `resources`, `events` `resources`, `metadata_exchange`, `qp_ready`. Initial state shows no pending data WR. Reveal INIT/RTR/RTS in compact detail; local transitions conceptual/source-derived, ready event recorded. Do not invent independently recorded intermediate state events. GID/IP/QPN/PSN label chips with exact values; direction A's destination QPN = B's local QPN and vice versa. No remote buffer address/RKEY exchanged for SEND. Primary **Choose the destination buffer**.
inspectCopy: The helper requests RC (Reliable Connected) QPs, one CQ for send and receive, capacity up to the requested eight send and eight receive WRs, one SGE per WR, and `sq_sig_all=1`. A provider may adjust actual capabilities. Those parameters are configuration, not counts of pending work. The ready log establishes preparation, not successful data transfer. [R1–R5]

title: Who decides where the message will land?
learnerCopy:
Think back to the TCP experiment. The receiver could delay calling `recv()`. The kernel's TCP socket could already contain unread bytes when we inspected it with `ss`.

RDMA SEND uses a different arrangement. Before a normal SEND arrives, the receiver needs to make suitable receive work available. The receiver chooses the memory in which the provider should place the incoming message. It describes that memory using its own local address, available length and LKEY. It then submits that description to its Receive Queue.

In this run the buffer can hold 4,096 bytes. That does not mean the sender has to transmit 4,096 bytes. It means that the receiver has supplied space for a message within that capacity. Our sender will send a much shorter message.

The program constructs an SGE (scatter/gather entry). An SGE identifies a range of locally registered memory. It then wraps that description in a Receive Work Request (`RecvWR`) and gives the request a local identifier. The identifier allows the receiving application to recognize the completion later. It is not an address on the network.

Calling `qp.post_recv(rwr)` submits the receive instruction. It does not itself move any payload. There is no new data packet simply because the receiver has posted this request. Once the receiver has posted the request, it sends the sender a `ready` message over the TCP control connection. The sender waits for that message before it starts the SEND.
visualSpec: Use actual B MR and receive WR `wr:b:hostb:exp-b-receiver:4`. Display a byte-buffer window with 4,096-byte capacity and zero-filled initial state labelled source-derived (`ctypes.create_string_buffer`), not a recorded initial snapshot. **Describe receive memory** highlights `exp_b_send_recv.py:104–106` and B address/LKEY/length. **Post receive request** highlights line 107 and places one instruction in B RQ; memory unchanged. **Tell A the receiver is ready** reveals line 112 and A `peer_ready` event `b:hosta:exp-b-sender:4`; dashed B→A TCP path. The posting log records submission, not queue occupancy measurements. No A SEND packet before this. Primary **Prepare the message on A**.
revealCopy: The receiver has prepared a destination. It has not received a message yet. The sender does not need to know B's destination virtual address or RKEY: B supplied that information locally through the receive request.

title: What if nobody has posted a receive?
learnerCopy:
Suppose A submits a normal RC SEND and B has no suitable receive request waiting. Where would B's provider put the incoming message? B has an RDMA endpoint, but it has not supplied a destination description for this operation.

This is different from TCP's ordinary socket buffering. A normal RC SEND that needs a receive request can encounter Receiver Not Ready, often abbreviated RNR. The receiving transport can respond that it is not ready to accept the message. The initiating transport may retry after a delay according to its configuration. With finite configured retries, failure can eventually be reported. A request can also remain outstanding while the application itself stops waiting.

In FabricLab's actual SEND program, B posts receive work before notifying A. That deliberately avoids this situation. We have no recorded RNR packet in the successful reference run, so we will illustrate the possible problem rather than pretend that we measured it.

There is another separate constraint: if the receive work exists but the supplied destination space is too small for the message, the operation can fail rather than behaving like a series of TCP `recv()` calls. The application must arrange suitable receive capacity.
visualSpec: Conceptual fork using five illustrative bytes only. Start with RQ empty. **Try SEND with no receive** shows "Receiver not ready" on the responder side, no successful placement or CQE, dashed reverse RNR explanation; no fake opcode/status/timing. **Prepare receive work** shows suitable local buffer description; **Return to recorded experiment** restores the real `send-recv` context. Optional **Inspect retry configuration** reveals helper lines 181,185–189 and explains `rnr_retry=7` permits indefinite RNR retries; the application helper has a finite wait timeout. No counter/timer simulation or fabricated failure capture. Primary **Construct the recorded SEND**.
revealCopy: A receive queue is not a store of arrived messages. It holds descriptions of where future eligible incoming messages may be placed. In the real run B prepares that description first. [R1, R3, R6]

references.title: NVIDIA RDMA-aware Networks Programming Guide; RDMAmojo practitioner notes

title: How does A construct and submit the actual SEND?
learnerCopy:
Now the receiving side is ready. The sender can prepare its own memory. The real program defines a bytes literal ending in a newline. It writes the message into its registered local buffer using `mr.write(...)`.

Do not confuse this call with an RDMA WRITE operation. Here `mr.write` is a local Pyverbs memory helper: the CPU executing the application puts bytes into the local buffer. There is no remote transfer yet. The actual RDMA operation is determined by the opcode in the Work Request that the application submits afterward.

The sender's SGE identifies the local starting address, message length and LKEY. The SendWR says which operation to perform, associates that SGE with the request and asks for successful completion reporting. The WR ID is chosen by the local program. In our run the opcode is SEND. The request has no remote-memory address or RKEY because the receive request at B supplies the destination.

Finally, `qp.post_send(swr)` submits the instruction to A's Send Queue. The function is named for the queue; later we will use it for WRITE and READ as well. Submission is asynchronous: a successful return does not by itself establish that the bytes have reached the other host. The application must observe completion and check its status before treating the operation as finished.
visualSpec: Use `exp_b_send_recv.py:43–45,128–145`. **Write bytes into A's buffer** shows true 50-byte payload from `b:packet:3.payloadHex` cross-checked with source bytes literal and B snapshot; label source contents reconstructed from code/packet, not a separately measured A memory snapshot. Display `\n` / hex `0a` explicitly; sender text log strips it. **Construct SEND instruction** highlights SGE fields and actual WR `wr:b:hosta:exp-b-sender:5`. **Submit to Send Queue** highlights line 139; constructed card moves to pending instruction state conceptually, source memory remains separate, B receive remains posted. Show no successful completion yet. Primary **Follow the data packet**.
inspectCopy: The lab logs a successful post call and uses a finite completion wait. A posting error and a later completion error are different failure stages. For this signalled non-inline operation, keep the registered buffer and relevant resources valid until completion is retrieved. The normal local key is not an RDMA transport-header field. [R1–R4, R7]

title: From local memory to a RoCEv2 packet
learnerCopy:
The provider now has an instruction and a way to access the source bytes. It also has a prepared peer endpoint. In the actual lab, software RXE uses the local memory description and executes the Reliable Connected transport through the Linux network path.

On the network we no longer see Python objects, addresses meaningful only to A's local CPU, or the local WR ID. We see a RoCEv2 request. The captured packet is addressed to B's data IP, uses UDP destination port 4791 and names B's destination QPN in its Base Transport Header (BTH).

The transport opcode says that this is a SEND message contained in one transport packet. The Packet Sequence Number (PSN) identifies its place in the transport's sequence. We will examine these fields in detail in Lesson 8. For now, the important point is that the packet identifies the communication endpoint and carries the message; it does not tell B an arbitrary virtual address to write to.

On B, the provider identifies the prepared QP, associates the SEND with the posted receive work, and places the message into the memory that B described. The receive work is consumed. This is a conceptual explanation of the transport mechanism; we did not instrument the exact moment a queue slot was retired or a RAM/cache location changed. The actual packet and later receive completion and buffer check are our evidence.
visualSpec: Use `b:packet:3` and both MR/WR records. **Inspect captured SEND** selects packet and reveals actual source/destination IP, UDP destination, opcode, destination QPN, PSN, payload hex/text and length breakdown. Display source memory → provider → packet → B provider → B memory as solid payload arrows; application → SQ and RQ → provider as separate instruction paths. **Follow placement at B** shows conceptual filled first 50 bytes, RQ instruction moves into consumed history; no claim of independently measured memory before completion. Label recorded packet vs causal illustration. Offer compact packet fields and full inspector/download, not mandatory full packet dump. Primary **Inspect transport acknowledgement**.
revealCopy: Why can the SEND packet omit B's virtual memory address? Because B's provider can find the receiving endpoint using the destination QPN and use the receive description that B already posted. The packet does not carry A's local LKEY or WR ID either.

title: The transport acknowledgement is not the application completion
learnerCopy:
We chose Reliable Connected transport. In our capture B responds to the SEND with a transport acknowledgement. The ACK travels from B to A, so its destination QPN identifies A, not B. It has no copy of the application message. The transport uses acknowledgement information to establish progress and support reliable delivery; it is not a Python message returned by `recv()`.

A completion is a different object. A provider reports the result of eligible local work in a Completion Queue. A polls its CQ to find out whether its SEND completed. B polls its own CQ to find out whether its posted RECEIVE completed. The two results refer to different locally chosen WR IDs and QPs, even though both relate to the same transfer.

A successful SEND completion in this RC example is not a promise that B's application has already examined, processed or acted on the message. The receiving application's own completion and subsequent verification establish that part of the story. In particular, we should not arrange the two CQ polls on one global timeline unless the evidence establishes that order.
visualSpec: **Inspect the reverse ACK** selects `b:packet:4`; reverse link, destination A QPN, ACK opcode, zero payload. Expand actual AETH fields if present in protocol tree. **Observe A's completion** reveals `cqe:b:hosta:exp-b-sender:6`. **Observe B's completion** independently reveals `cqe:b:hostb:exp-b-receiver:5`. Both controls independently available after transport stage. Show conceptual CQ entry → poll → observed WC outside CQ; actual log records retrieval, not queue occupancy. Each local timeline independent; no forced A-before-B ordering. Show real WR IDs, local QPNs, statuses, opcodes. Primary **Read B's verified memory** after B completion revealed (allow review/skip explanation without falsely marking evidence observed).
inspectCopy: The program's polling helper returns a WC only after SUCCESS, otherwise raises on error or after a timeout. Inspect `rdma_common.py:194–224`. Use the receive WC's `byte_len` to determine received message length. The fixture also records a send-side `byte_len`; label it as a recorded RXE result, not a portable SEND/WRITE completion-length contract. General software should not depend on send-side `byte_len` as proof of remote memory contents. [R3, R7]

title: Read the memory that B actually received
learnerCopy:
B's application has now retrieved its successful receive completion. It uses the received byte count to decide how many bytes to inspect in its buffer. Notice that this is not another socket `recv()` call. The RDMA provider has already placed the message in the memory B supplied. The program reads its own buffer using ordinary CPU memory access.

The actual source uses `bytes(buf.raw[:n])`. In Python, producing this bytes object can itself involve a local copy. That is application processing after the RDMA operation, not another network transfer. The program compares the received bytes with the expected literal and records whether the lengths and contents match.

Our evidence shows a 50-byte message, even though the receive buffer had capacity for 4,096 bytes. The packet carries exactly those message bytes, including the final newline. Transport padding is not part of the message. We have not captured every byte of the remaining destination buffer and should not present those bytes as independently measured.

We now have several complementary observations: the request was submitted, the SEND packet was captured, the receiver reported a successful completion, and the application verified the resulting data. Together they establish what this experiment accomplished.
visualSpec: Use `exp_b_send_recv.py:113–121` and `b:memory:hostb:received`, `b:hostb:exp-b-receiver:7`. **Read received bytes** shows actual memory snapshot with offsets, ASCII/hex toggle, newline visible. Compare full unpadded packet bytes with snapshot, show exact equality and 50/4096 distinction derived from evidence. Remaining buffer capacity shown as unobserved in snapshot, not drawn as captured zeros. Display local sequence B completion → read → verify, independent A SEND completion. **Compare with TCP** reveals the authored comparison below. Primary **Review the SEND experiment** advances to 5.9.
revealCopy: TCP gives an application an ordered byte stream; individual writes and reads may have different boundaries. In this RC SEND example, B prepared receive work for one message, and the receive completion identifies the received message length. Both can transport the same bytes, but the application interface and the way destination memory is supplied are different. Next we will let A name B's remote memory directly.

title: Review: reconstruct the SEND experiment
learnerCopy:
Before moving on, see if you can explain the transfer without relying on the names of the API calls. B decided where to put the message. A decided which message to send. The providers used their prepared endpoints to communicate. The receiving provider placed the bytes in B's registered buffer, and both applications observed their own work completions.

Now imagine you only have the captured SEND packet. Can you find B's application buffer address in it? Can you establish that B has actually consumed the data? We need more than the network capture to answer those questions.
visualSpec: One compact review, no new timeline. Present `b:packet:3` without answer-bearing heading other than decoded fields. Question 1 options **From RETH**, **From B's posted receive work**, **From UDP destination port**. Correct: B's posted receive work. Question 2 options **SEND packet alone**, **B's successful completion and verified buffer**, **A's WR ID alone**. Correct: B's evidence. Allow **Reveal explanation** and **Skip review** without mastery claim. Show missing receive, local instruction, network request, observed completion and verified data in a single causal strip with labels. Final **Continue to ordinary RDMA WRITE** calls lesson completion. If direct-reference mode has unvisited sections, provide explicit review/reference navigation rather than marking lesson complete.
revealCopy: There is no RETH in this captured ordinary SEND. The receiver's local instruction supplies the address. A packet can show a message crossing the capture point, but the receive completion and verified bytes are additional application evidence. We are ready to ask whether a sender could choose the remote destination instead.

title: The question that SEND leaves unanswered
learnerCopy:
In the preceding experiment, B's application chose the destination buffer before A submitted its SEND. B posted receive work and the receiving provider consumed that work when the message arrived. Each application observed a local completion for its own request.

What if the two applications agree in advance on a region of memory that A is allowed to update? Instead of asking B to supply a new receive description for every message, A could name an authorized destination inside that region. That is the ordinary RDMA WRITE operation we will study now.

The word ordinary is important. We mean RDMA WRITE without immediate data, not every possible WRITE variant. The target still needs a prepared endpoint and a registered region with appropriate access. The target application must cooperate in establishing that access and coordinating use of the buffer. It simply does not need to post a receive WR for each ordinary WRITE.

One-sided does not mean that only one computer exists, that no target setup is required, or that the target CPU does nothing for the entire program. It describes the interface for this data operation: the initiator can request access to already authorized remote memory without the target application submitting a matching receive instruction for that operation.

We will compare the same basic objective — data in A's memory appears in B's memory — using a separate, genuine WRITE run.
visualSpec: Reuse stable two-host layout. Start with compact **Recall SEND** diagram (B chooses destination via RQ). **Compare ordinary WRITE** swaps destination-selection relation: A names region on B, B RQ has no receive posted for this operation. Use only illustrative HELLO in this comparison, explicitly not the two recorded runs. Distinct instruction and payload paths; no packet or result before setup. Then **Open the recorded WRITE experiment** switches to `write` run, with role labels writer/target. Show new evidence badge and distinct run ID; no mixing of QPNs or keys across runs.
revealCopy: The difference is not that SEND cannot place data in registered memory. Both operations can do that. The difference is who supplies the destination description and whether matching receive work is required.

title: Prepare B's memory and advertise only what A needs
learnerCopy:
The actual WRITE program, `exp_c_write.py`, runs a writer on A and a target on B. It creates its resources in much the same way as the SEND program. There is one important addition: the target initializes its buffer with dots before registration, so later it can demonstrate that its contents have changed.

B records the first 64 bytes of this initial buffer. The dots are actual ASCII bytes (`0x2e`), not empty or unallocated memory. The full buffer has room for 4,096 bytes. B registers the range using the helper we saw earlier; the fixture enables local write, remote write and remote read access. It also prepares QP access attributes. In a real application, access should be limited to what the operation requires.

During the TCP metadata exchange, both hosts share their endpoint identity. In addition, B shares its registered address, RKEY and available length. A does not need B's local key to issue a remote WRITE. B's local key and remote key happen to have equal numeric values in this reference run; equality is not a protocol requirement and the two fields have different roles.

The programs then prepare their RC endpoints. B sends `ready` over the control socket. This readiness tells A that the target has prepared the necessary resources; it does not mean B posted a Receive Work Request. In this experiment it never posts one for the ordinary WRITE.
visualSpec: Evidence `write.endpoints`, `c:memory:hostb:before`, `c:hostb:exp-c-target:2–4`, `c:hosta:exp-c-writer:2–4`. **Inspect target before** displays first 64 captured snapshot bytes, address/capacity; remainder not sampled. **Share destination information** highlights `exp_c_write.py:57–69,106–109`; actual B→A tuple address/RKEY/length on dashed TCP lane, both endpoint tuples in expandable detail. **Prepare endpoints and signal readiness** uses lines 111–122,152–157, actual A `peer_ready`. Show B RQ with no receive WR for this experiment, as supported by source/WR evidence, not a continuously sampled empty queue. Source `rdma_common.py:131–151,166–191` for MR/QP access and CQ associations; inspect actual `ACCESS` constant from embedded source using exact symbol match, not invented flags. Primary **Build A's WRITE instruction**.
inspectCopy: Registration relates an address range to a PD and access keys. Remote access also depends on endpoint configuration and provider checks. The target's address is meaningful in its registered-memory context; A's CPU cannot simply load or store through that virtual address. [R4, R5, R8]

references.title: Linux rdma-core, Pyverbs and RXE documentation

title: Build a WRITE instruction from two memory descriptions
learnerCopy:
A has two different pieces of information to assemble. The first describes its own memory: the source address, the local key and the number of bytes to transfer. The second identifies the remote destination: B's registered address and RKEY.

The program puts its bytes literal into A's own registered buffer using `mr.write(...)`. This is an ordinary local memory helper, not the network WRITE. The message is 53 bytes including the newline. The actual network request begins when the application constructs a SendWR with opcode `IBV_WR_RDMA_WRITE` and submits it to the Send Queue.

Notice the extra call compared with SEND:

```python
swr.set_wr_rdma(rkey=peer["rkey"], addr=peer["addr"])
```

The remote key and address come from the target's earlier metadata exchange. The transfer length comes from the local SGE, not from a second independent remote length parameter. The advertised target length is a useful bound for the application to respect; it is not automatically substituted for the number of bytes in this WRITE. The provider checks the actual registered range and permissions when carrying out the operation.

The WR ID is local to A. The local LKEY is used to describe A's registered source. Neither is a field that B needs to receive over the network in this ordinary WRITE. The remote address and RKEY, by contrast, are part of the request that the transport must deliver to the target.
visualSpec: Use `exp_c_write.py:124–138` and `wr:c:hosta:exp-c-writer:5`. **Fill A's source buffer** displays `c:packet:7.payloadHex` with newline; source-derived/reconstructed not sampled A RAM. **Describe local source** reveals SGE and source address/LKEY/length. **Add remote destination** reveals `set_wr_rdma` source line and B's shared tuple, with different colors and explicit owner labels. **Construct WRITE instruction** reveals opcode, WR ID and signalled property; no pending SQ entry until submission. **Submit WRITE** highlights line 134 and adds pending conceptual instruction. No destination memory verification yet. Primary **Follow the WRITE packet**.
revealCopy: What changed from SEND? A added an operation code selecting WRITE and a remote-memory description. B did not supply receive work. A still uses its own local memory description; it does not use B's RKEY as a local LKEY.

title: What does the target provider do with the incoming request?
learnerCopy:
The provider on A has the local data and prepared connection information. It constructs the transport request. Because the operation is WRITE, the request contains a remote-memory header in addition to the base transport header. We call that extension RETH, the RDMA Extended Transport Header.

RETH identifies the remote virtual address, RKEY and transfer length. B's transport can use the destination QPN to find the receiving endpoint context, interpret the opcode and check whether the requested remote access is allowed. The request must match suitable registered memory and lie within its permitted range. A valid address alone is not sufficient, and a valid key alone is not sufficient.

After these checks, the target provider places the bytes into the specified portion of B's registered buffer. No ordinary receive WR is consumed. In the lab this is software RXE processing on B's CPU; the representative hardware-RNIC implementation performs the equivalent transport and memory-placement work in the device. Do not confuse the two implementations.

The captured WRITE fits in one transport packet. The provider is not transferring the Python object itself or a copy of B's key table. It transfers the message and enough transport information for the target to perform the permitted memory access.
visualSpec: Select actual `c:packet:7`. **Inspect WRITE request** displays outer network destination, BTH destination QPN/opcode/PSN and RETH address/RKEY/DMA length, payload and length breakdown. **Check target access** highlights corresponding B registration, requested byte interval `[address,address+length)` and MR/QP access flags from source; successful checks are causal explanation consistent with verified run, not independently logged per-check results. **Follow target placement** illustrates first 53 bytes becoming message; RQ unchanged; target observation explicitly "placement illustrated; actual buffer check not yet revealed". Do not draw the payload through SQ or RQ. No fabricated target CQE. Primary **Follow the reverse acknowledgement**.
inspectCopy: For a multi-packet ordinary WRITE, not every packet has a RETH; the first (or only) WRITE packet carries the remote-memory description. Later packets belong to the same transport operation. Our capture has one WRITE Only packet. [R1, R9–R12]

IANA service name and transport protocol registry
IBTA specification access; original RDMAmojo QP transport discussion

title: What did the writer actually learn from completion?
learnerCopy:
B sends a transport acknowledgement back to A. Like the ACK in SEND, it is addressed to A's QP, not B's QP. It is part of the RC transport, not a reply message constructed by B's Python application. The ACK does not carry the 53-byte application message.

A polls its CQ. The recorded result is SUCCESS for the WRITE WR ID. In this particular RC host-memory experiment, it establishes successful completion of the requested transport operation from the initiator's point of view. It permits A to reuse the relevant source buffer according to the operation and registration lifetime rules.

It does not establish that B's Python application has read the destination, performed further computation or saved anything durably. Completion is not a general memory-persistence guarantee. Other memory types and relaxed-ordering or accelerator configurations may require additional ordering and synchronization mechanisms.

This distinction is easy to miss because the word complete sounds like the whole application workflow has finished. It has not. A knows its operation completed; B still needs a way to learn when it may use the incoming data.
visualSpec: **Inspect the ACK** shows `c:packet:8` reverse direction and actual decoded AETH if available, no application payload or RETH. **Poll writer CQ** reveals `cqe:c:hosta:exp-c-writer:6`, then `c:hosta:exp-c-writer:7` write_complete. Show retrieved completion outside CQ, conceptual pending entry not claimed measured. Use `exp_c_write.py:140–145` and shared poll helper. Keep target CQ observation unrevealed, target memory verification unrevealed. Primary **Predict how B learns the result**.
revealCopy: If you were debugging only from the network, an ACK would be a valuable transport observation. It would not show the target application's later verification. The application and the transport have different responsibilities. [R1, R3, R7]

title: Does B receive a normal completion when its memory changes?
learnerCopy:
Suppose you are writing the target application. In the SEND experiment you could poll your receive CQ to learn that your posted receive work completed. Can you do the same thing for this ordinary WRITE?

Make a prediction before looking at the evidence. Remember that B did not submit a Receive Work Request for this operation. A submitted a WRITE against B's registered memory.

The memory being updated and the application being notified are two distinct events. A provider can perform a remote memory operation without completing a local receive instruction. The mechanism for telling B's application that it is safe to inspect the data must be part of the application protocol.
visualSpec: Show B registered destination, no receive WR for operation, B CQ **not inspected yet**, no recorded after snapshot. Prompt **Will ordinary WRITE produce a normal receive completion at B?** Options **Yes**, **No**, **Not sure**; optional **Skip prediction**. Do not reveal correct answer on selection. Store choice scoped to subsection/revision. **Follow the synchronization message** reveals A source line 150 only after writer completion (recap prerequisite even on direct section access); B receives `c:hostb:exp-c-target:5` on dashed TCP lane. **Poll B's CQ** reveals `c:hostb:exp-c-target:6` actual `npolled=0`, line 161; no global claim that all future polls are empty. Feedback below follows observation. Primary **Read B's buffer**.
revealCopy: The recorded poll returned zero entries. Ordinary WRITE does not produce a normal target receive completion just because data was placed in memory. The successful initiator completion and the explicit control message are what allow this test program to coordinate its verification. B could have unrelated CQ entries in a more complex program; the observation here is one specific poll in a controlled run.

title: Where did the data go if B's completion queue is empty?
learnerCopy:
Now look at B's memory. Its initial snapshot contains dots. After A observes its successful WRITE completion, it sends the small JSON message `{"write_done": true}` on the TCP control connection. B receives that message, polls its CQ once and then reads the beginning of its own buffer.

The control message does not carry the WRITE payload and does not cause the placement. It tells the target application that the writer has completed the operation and that the test may inspect the memory. The data was transferred through the RDMA data network. This is why we keep the control and data paths separate.

The actual program reads exactly the number of expected payload bytes. It compares them against the expected literal and records a successful match together with the zero-entry target CQ observation. We can now see the message in B's memory even though there was no ordinary receive completion on B.

The before event contains the first 64 bytes. Despite the field name `first64` in the after event, the program actually records 53 bytes after the WRITE because it slices to the payload length. We must compare the common observed range, not claim that the after log sampled the remaining eleven bytes. This is a good example of why reading the program matters when interpreting a log.
visualSpec: Evidence `c:memory:hostb:before`, `c:memory:hostb:after`, `c:hostb:exp-c-target:5,6,7`; source `exp_c_write.py:147–171`. **Inspect before and after** displays aligned byte cells for common 53-byte range; before includes expandable extra sampled 11 dots, after beyond 53 labelled not observed. Compare after hex against `c:packet:7.payloadHex` including newline. Show target local order signal → poll zero → memory verification. Display actual result `payload_ok`, `target_cqe_count`, `ok`. Keep ordinary CPU read path distinct from RDMA memory placement. Primary **Compare SEND and WRITE**.
revealCopy: If the target application only waited for an ordinary receive CQE, it would not receive notification of this WRITE through that mechanism. Software must agree on how to signal ownership and readiness of the buffer. [R1, R3, R7]

title: Compare SEND, WRITE and notification choices
learnerCopy:
We have now seen two ways to place a message in B's memory. In both cases A submits work on its Send Queue and the transport moves application data from A to B. The most important difference is the destination-selection rule.

In SEND, B chooses where incoming data goes by posting receive work. A does not include a remote address and RKEY for that operation. A's SEND and B's RECEIVE each produce the corresponding local completion in our signalled experiment.

In ordinary WRITE, A names an authorized region on B. A includes a remote address and RKEY, and B does not need a matching receive WR for that operation. The successful initiator completion does not become a normal receive completion at B. Our lab uses a separate TCP notification after completion so B can inspect the result.

There are other ways for applications to arrange notification. For example, WRITE with immediate data is a distinct operation that can supply a receive completion carrying immediate information on the target side, and requires suitable posted receive work there. The WRITE payload still goes to the named remote region, not to the receive WR's data buffer as if it were a SEND. That is not the operation we captured. Another design might use a follow-up message or carefully designed shared-memory signaling protocol. Such designs must respect ordering, synchronization and memory visibility rules.

For this lesson, remember the simplest distinction: **remote memory placement does not automatically imply remote application notification**.
visualSpec: Two-column comparison with fixed A/B host positions, selector **SEND**, **Ordinary WRITE**, **Inspect WRITE with immediate (conceptual)** (optional expansion only). Display actual SEND/WRITE reference results separately, no mixed QPNs. Show destination selection, matching receive requirement, transmitted RETH, local completion ownership, target notification. For immediate variant show conceptual RQ consumption and immediate metadata in receive WC, no fabricated opcode or capture. Short prediction: **Which evidence proves B's bytes matched?** options ACK alone / B's buffer verification / A's LKEY. Correct B buffer verification. Final **Continue to RDMA READ** via curriculum completion callback.
revealCopy: SEND lets the receiver choose the buffer for a message. Ordinary WRITE lets the initiator name a permitted destination. WRITE with immediate is a different operation and cannot be used to explain the observed zero target CQEs in our ordinary WRITE run. [R1–R3, R6]

title: Change the question: who already has the data?
learnerCopy:
In SEND and WRITE, A had the message and wanted to place it in B's memory. Suppose instead that B already has data which A needs. Perhaps B is holding a portion of an array and A wants to retrieve it into a local buffer.

One possible design is to send B a request message and have B's application issue a SEND reply. That is an application-level request/reply protocol. But if B has registered an authorized region for remote reads, A can request the data directly through an RDMA READ. B's provider services the request using the prepared transport and memory-access context; B's application does not have to submit a new SendWR for the response.

This gives us four separate roles to track. Which host initiates the operation? Which host contains the source data? Which host receives the data? Which application observes completion? In our READ experiment, A initiates, B supplies the data, A receives it, and A observes its READ completion.

The distinction matters because the first packet travels from A to B, whereas the data returns from B to A. A is using its Send Queue even though its local memory is the destination of the payload.
visualSpec: Conceptual fixed A/B diagram: B contains HELLO, A zero buffer. **Compare application request/reply** shows two application-controlled SEND messages in illustration only. **Choose RDMA READ** shows A's instruction, request arrow A→B, response arrow B→A, A completion. Separate arrows labelled request / payload. Do not imply B executes `post_send()` for response. **Open the recorded READ experiment** switches to `read`, roles reader/source. New run scope and fresh resource metadata.
revealCopy: The word sender can be ambiguous in READ: A transmits the request, B transmits the response containing the data. Use reader/initiator and source/responder rather than calling both hosts sender.

title: Prepare a source and a destination
learnerCopy:
Our actual program is `exp_d_read.py`. On B, the source process allocates a 4,096-byte buffer, fills it with `#` bytes, registers it and puts a known message into the beginning of the registered memory. That message contains 46 bytes including a newline. The recorded initial snapshot shows the message followed by hash characters.

On A, the reader allocates and registers its own 4,096-byte buffer. That is where the response data should land. In READ, A's local SGE will describe a destination rather than a source. The provider must be able to write into that local destination, so the applicable local-write access is important. B must have authorized remote-read access to the source. The shared registration helper enables both in the reference lab, along with remote-write access; a production design should grant only necessary access.

B shares the remote address, RKEY and the available data length with A over the control connection. This time the advertised length is the length of the valid message, not the full 4,096-byte registration. That is an application decision: the receiver of metadata needs to know how much meaningful data the source intends to expose. It must still keep requests within the registered range.

The programs prepare their QPs and B signals readiness. The resources are new for this READ run, so we will not reuse addresses or QPNs from the previous WRITE.
visualSpec: **Inspect B's source** uses `d:memory:hostb:before`, displays 64 sampled bytes: first 46 message including newline, next 18 hashes. **Prepare A's destination** shows actual MR metadata and source-derived zero-initialized buffer (no recorded before snapshot A). **Exchange source metadata** shows `exp_d_read.py:90–106`, B `d:hostb:exp-d-source:3` shared length 46 vs MR length 4096, A peer data; dashed TCP lane. **Confirm readiness** uses source 137 and A event `d:hosta:exp-d-reader:4`. Show access roles local destination write on A, remote source read on B and QP access context. No B RQ or SQ WR submitted for servicing this operation. Primary **Describe a READ**.
inspectCopy: Source code `exp_d_read.py:61–82` establishes allocation and source initialization. The B snapshot is observed after initialization; the A zero buffer is inferred from allocation, not independently sampled. Distinguish buffer capacity, advertised data length and requested length. [R4, R5]

title: Why does the reader use a Send Work Request?
learnerCopy:
The name `SendWR` may seem odd now. We want A to receive data. Why would the reader use `SendWR` and call `post_send()`?

The Send Queue is the queue on which an application submits initiated operations. Those operations can send a message, write remote memory or request a remote read, depending on the opcode and QP type. The word Send in the API name is describing the queue, not necessarily the direction of the eventual payload.

The reader constructs an SGE using its own buffer address, length and LKEY. For a READ this is the local destination. It constructs a SendWR with opcode `IBV_WR_RDMA_READ`, a local WR ID and a request for completion reporting. Then it sets the remote source address and RKEY from the earlier metadata exchange.

Once A calls `qp.post_send(swr)`, its provider has enough information to request the remote data and place the returned bytes into the correct local region. The local destination address and LKEY stay part of A's local work context. B does not need to receive them to service the READ.
visualSpec: Use `exp_d_read.py:110–124`, `wr:d:hosta:exp-d-reader:5`. **Describe local destination** highlights SGE and A memory; label arrow as destination reference (not outgoing payload). **Name remote source** shows `set_wr_rdma` with B address/RKEY. **Construct READ** reveals actual opcode, WR ID and length. **Submit to A's Send Queue** shows conceptual pending WR and keeps A buffer unmodified. Include same source lines as WRITE in optional compare but never mix actual runtime values. Primary **Follow the request to B**.
revealCopy: SEND and WRITE use the local SGE as a data source; READ uses the local SGE as a destination. All three are initiated through the Send Queue in this RC program. The opcode determines the operation. [R1, R4]

title: Follow the request: A asks, but sends no message payload
learnerCopy:
The first captured READ packet goes from A to B. Its opcode says RDMA READ Request. It identifies B's QP and contains a RETH that names the remote source address, remote key and requested byte count.

This packet is unlike the SEND and WRITE request packets we have already seen. It contains a request for data, not the 46 bytes themselves. The amount requested is in RETH, even though the packet has no application payload.

At B, the provider uses the endpoint context and remote-memory description to check whether the requested region can be read. It can then obtain the data from the authorized source. In the actual Soft-RoCE lab, software performs this transport processing; in the representative hardware model, the RNIC performs the equivalent operation using device access to registered memory.

B does not have to wait for its application to notice the READ packet and manually construct a reply. The prepared transport handles the response. No ordinary receive WR is consumed by the READ request, and no new application SendWR is needed to produce the response.
visualSpec: **Inspect captured READ request** uses `d:packet:3`. Display BTH, RETH, zero payload, requested length 46 derived from evidence. **Check remote source** highlights B MR and requested range, permission; label causal check not logged per step. A destination still not verified. Draw A→B request with dashed or explicitly labelled instruction/transport arrow; not a payload arrow. B source bytes stay unchanged in conceptual model (no post-read B memory sample claim). Primary **Follow the response back to A**.
revealCopy: A request can describe a 46-byte transfer without carrying any of those 46 bytes. Inspect the opcode and header structure before interpreting the packet's application data length. [R1, R9–R12]

title: Follow the response: B supplies data to A
learnerCopy:
The second packet in our READ evidence is a response. It comes from B and is addressed to A's QP. The destination QPN has changed because the packet direction has changed. The response's opcode identifies a complete single-packet READ response.

It carries the data requested by A. It does not repeat the remote address and RKEY from the request as a RETH. A's provider has an outstanding READ context describing where to place the returned bytes. That context includes A's local SGE; the packet does not need to transmit A's local LKEY or destination virtual address.

The provider places the data into A's registered destination. Our diagram illustrates this memory placement. The subsequent completion and application verification are the recorded observations. We are not measuring the precise physical moment at which each cache line or memory location changes.

A READ does not mean moving the original object out of B's memory. It obtains a copy of bytes from the source. The initial source snapshot in this run contains the expected message; the reference does not record a later B-memory comparison, so we will not claim to have measured the entire unchanged source after the READ.
visualSpec: **Inspect captured READ response** selects `d:packet:4`. Show B→A payload arrow distinct from previous A→B request; A QPN, opcode, PSN, AETH if exported, no RETH, payload including newline. **Place returned bytes** illustrates destination memory first 46 bytes; keep label causal until application reads. Compare payload hex to B initial snapshot prefix, not trailing hashes or padding. Show A's pending WR context linking response to local destination. No B application SEND instruction. Primary **Observe the reader's completion**.
revealCopy: The provider on B sends the response as part of servicing A's operation. The application that initiated the READ is still A. Packet source, data source and operation initiator are different roles.

title: Observe completion and verify the actual local data
learnerCopy:
A polls its CQ and obtains a successful RDMA READ Work Completion. The local WR ID identifies the original request. The result tells the reader that the operation has completed. In this case the completion reports the transferred length, and the program uses that to read its own buffer.

Only after observing completion does the program read and compare the bytes with the expected message. The recorded `read_complete` event contains the data and a successful verification. Reading that Python buffer is ordinary local CPU memory access after the network transfer. The result is a local copy of bytes that were stored on the other machine.

Now consider B's application. It provided registered source memory and coordinated the experiment. Did it get a normal local completion for servicing A's ordinary READ? No matching local WR was submitted. The ordinary READ responder does not receive a normal CQE simply because a remote peer read its memory.

The actual program makes this observable: after A has verified the data, it sends `{"read_done": true}` over the TCP control connection. B receives it and polls its CQ once. That poll returns zero entries in this run. This is a distinct, later observation, not something we measured when the response packet was first seen.
visualSpec: **Poll reader CQ** reveals `cqe:d:hosta:exp-d-reader:6`; no pending CQE after poll. **Inspect verified reader memory** uses `d:memory:hosta:read-result`, `d:hosta:exp-d-reader:7` and `exp_d_read.py:126–130`; compare response payload and source snapshot prefix with verified A bytes. **Signal READ done** reveals source line 134 and B `d:hostb:exp-d-source:5`. **Inspect source CQ** reveals `d:hostb:exp-d-source:6`, source lines 137–144; not before synchronization. Show B's poll returning zero at this point, no universal empty-queue assertion. Primary **Compare the three operations**.
inspectCopy: The lab uses an explicit synchronization message to coordinate verification and shutdown. It does not carry the data or cause the READ response. Applications must keep source/destination memory valid for outstanding work and coordinate access and reuse. [R1–R4, R7]

title: Put the three operations side by side
learnerCopy:
We can now describe the three operations without memorizing API class names. Ask who supplies the data, who selects the destination, what memory metadata is required and which application receives a local completion.

For ordinary SEND, A supplies the message and B chooses its destination with a posted receive description. For ordinary WRITE, A supplies data and names an authorized destination at B. For READ, A names an authorized source at B and supplies its own local destination. The request goes outward and the payload comes back.

The transport uses endpoint context for all three. It can acknowledge or respond as required by the operation. A local Work Completion is the application-facing result of eligible work, not a network packet. We used signalled operations and recorded successful completions in this lab; more advanced programs may use selective signalling and different CQ associations.

None of these facts tells us that every RDMA-based library uses one particular operation. A library can choose operations, queue layouts and synchronization strategies to meet its needs. But if you know these basic mechanisms, you have the tools to understand why a library might use them.
visualSpec:
Use this authored comparison, responsive rows with fixed A/B icons; use recorded counts separately and exact `write` ordinary semantics:

| Question | SEND | Ordinary WRITE | READ |
|---|---|---|---|
| Initiator in our lab | A | A | A |
| Application payload | A → B | A → B | B → A |
| Who describes destination? | B, posted receive | A, remote address and RKEY | A, local SGE |
| Matching target receive WR? | Yes | No | No |
| Remote address and RKEY in request? | No | Yes, destination | Yes, source |
| Local completions recorded | A SEND; B RECEIVE | A WRITE | A READ |
| Target application coordination | Posted receive, then observe receive completion | Explicit control notification in this run | Source readiness and done synchronization in this run |

Optional **Trace one operation** selector highlights initiator, request direction, payload direction, memory destination and completion ownership. Short prompt **A posts READ. Which direction does the payload move?** A→B / B→A / neither. Correct B→A. Primary **Investigate the packets on the wire** via curriculum completion callback.
revealCopy: The request direction follows the initiator. The payload direction follows where the bytes reside and where they must go. Next we will work backwards from packets to the operations that generated them.

title: What exactly are we looking at in a packet capture?
learnerCopy:
We have followed three real operations. We know where the data starts, which application submits work and how the result is observed. Now we will look at the same experiments from the point of view of a network engineer who sees packets but may not have access to the application.

Start with the familiar part of the captured SEND packet. An Ethernet header identifies the local link delivery. The IPv4 header identifies the network source and destination. Its protocol field says the payload is UDP. The UDP destination port is 4791, the registered port for RoCEv2. This tells us how the RDMA transport is encapsulated for IP networking.

UDP is not providing the reliable connection semantics that TCP provides. In our experiment the Reliable Connected RDMA transport carries its own sequencing, acknowledgement and retry mechanisms inside the UDP payload. The data path is not a TCP stream. The TCP control socket we used for setup is a separate conversation.

A network device that forwards this IP traffic need not interpret every RDMA header. The outer addresses and other forwarding information can be sufficient. At the destination, the RDMA transport interprets the inner header and directs the operation to the appropriate endpoint.

We will use FabricLab's packet inspector, which displays fields decoded from genuine captured traffic. It is not a screenshot of Wireshark. You can download the original PCAP and open it in Wireshark to inspect the same frames yourself.
visualSpec: Open `b:packet:3` by default. Show actual Ethernet II, IPv4, UDP and BTH header strips in byte order; clicking a strip reveals the corresponding existing `protocolTree` fields and points to relevant byte spans in `rawHex` when verified offsets are available. **Follow Ethernet delivery**, **Follow IP delivery**, **Open UDP encapsulation**, **Inspect the RDMA header** progressively highlight the selected layer, preserving outer context. For actual captured Ethernet/IPv4 header sizes verify bytes (EtherType, IPv4 IHL etc.) rather than assume all networks have the same header size. Show data/control topology inset. Link actual PCAP. No invented GUI screenshot. Primary **Understand endpoint and operation fields**.
inspectCopy: RoCEv1 uses a different Ethernet encapsulation; RoCEv2 adds IP and UDP so it can be routed at Layer 3. This curriculum focuses on the IPv4 RoCEv2 RC evidence, not every InfiniBand transport service. [R9–R13]

title: How does the receiving transport know what to do?
learnerCopy:
Immediately after the UDP header we encounter the Base Transport Header, or BTH. Think of it as the common part of the RDMA transport packet. It identifies the operation and contains information the transport needs to interpret and sequence that packet.

Start with the destination QPN. We learned in the resource lesson that a Queue Pair has an endpoint number. In the SEND capture, this field names B's QP. In the reverse acknowledgement it names A's QP. It is not the local WR ID or a TCP port. For RC, the endpoint has been prepared with peer information; a receiving provider knows which context to use for the arriving packet. There is no independent source-QPN field in the ordinary RC BTH of these packets. Use the endpoint metadata and operation context to identify the peer, not an imaginary field.

The opcode tells the transport how to interpret what follows the BTH. The verbs opcode in a Work Request identifies the requested operation, while the packet opcode identifies a particular transport packet form. For example, a SEND Work Request can generate a SEND Only packet when its message fits in one packet, or a sequence of SEND First, Middle and Last packets for a longer message. The opcode also determines which extension headers are present.

The PSN is a 24-bit packet sequence number. It helps the RC transport track packet progress. The applications configure an initial sequence value while preparing their endpoints; the provider uses transport sequencing during execution. A PSN is not an application byte offset and is not the application's WR ID.
visualSpec: Show three linked selectable fields from the actual SEND request: **Destination QPN**, **Opcode**, **PSN**. QPN selection highlights B endpoint using validated correlation and B local QPN; **Switch to ACK** highlights A endpoint and actual reverse packet fields. Opcode links actual SEND WR vs wire SEND Only; ACK is a transport response, not a new application WR. PSN selection connects initial peer sequence setup to observed request and ACK, scoped to this single-packet run. Include decimal/hex toggle without losing labels. If P_Key, AckReq and pad count are shown, use the exact decoded fields; explain their roles in inspect panel rather than equate them with security credentials. Primary **Open remote memory fields**.
inspectCopy: The BTH also carries such information as a partition key, a request-for-acknowledgement bit and a pad count. The partition key is a transport partition identifier, not an MR RKEY. AckReq is not the packet being an ACK. In these RC captures, the ACK packet's own opcode identifies acknowledgement. [R9–R12]

title: When does an RDMA packet contain a remote memory address?
learnerCopy:
Compare a SEND request with a WRITE request. They both carry application bytes from A to B. Their BTH opcodes differ, and the WRITE request includes an extra header, the RDMA Extended Transport Header (RETH).

A WRITE needs to identify an authorized destination. RETH contains a 64-bit virtual address, a 32-bit RKEY and a 32-bit DMA length. These fields describe the remote-memory operation in the context of the receiving endpoint and registered memory. The address is not a network IP address. The key is not a UDP port, encryption key or proof of general host identity.

An RDMA READ Request also contains RETH, but its remote address names the source rather than the destination. Its length describes how much data is requested, even though the request carries no application message bytes. In the READ response we do not need to repeat RETH; the reader already has the outstanding operation context and its local destination description.

A SEND request does not contain RETH because B has already supplied its own destination through receive work. A transport ACK does not contain RETH either. The particular extensions are determined by the packet opcode, not by the assumption that every RoCEv2 packet carries all possible fields.
visualSpec: Four mutually exclusive packet selectors **SEND request**, **WRITE request**, **READ request**, **READ response**, plus **ACK**. Use `b:packet:3`, `c:packet:7`, `d:packet:3`, `d:packet:4`, `c:packet:8`. Show real `protocolTree` and optional `reth` field only when present. RETH selection highlights B memory interval for WRITE or READ, with operation-specific role. For SEND show B receive WR as the address source outside packet; for response show A local WR context; for ACK no memory field. Preserve run identity and A/B direction. Primary **Compare message length and packet length**.
revealCopy: A packet can carry payload without RETH (SEND or READ response), and it can carry RETH without payload (READ Request). The presence of a remote-memory description and the presence of message data are separate questions. [R1, R9–R12]

title: Count the bytes: buffer capacity, transfer length, padding and frame size
learnerCopy:
Earlier we saw a 4,096-byte registered buffer used for a 50-byte SEND. That is one of several different lengths that appear while inspecting a transfer.

The registered length bounds memory access. An SGE describes the portion involved in the operation. The receiving application's completion or verification establishes how many bytes it actually obtained in our SEND example. The frame on the wire contains not only application bytes but protocol headers and other transport fields.

RoCE transport may add padding to align its data portion. Our SEND message contains 50 bytes, including a newline. The capture has two additional padding bytes in the data portion. The WRITE message is 53 bytes with three padding bytes. The READ response has 46 message bytes and two padding bytes. The padding is not part of the Python message, and it is not part of the registered memory write length. The READ request has no payload at all despite asking for 46 bytes.

When you compare a captured frame with application memory, use the unpadded application payload. The last `0a` in these messages is a newline in the original bytes literal, not padding. A human-readable log may have stripped it from its text representation, so a comparison based only on the displayed string can give the wrong answer.
visualSpec: Use existing `packetLengthBreakdown()` and actual evidence. One horizontal byte strip per selected packet, show headers, app payload, padding and transport integrity/other fields only when independently decoded or explicitly derived. Use actual captured frame length and captured length, not an assumed physical on-wire Ethernet preamble/FCS count. For SEND: verify expected app 50, pad 2, data 52, frame 110; WRITE 53/3/56/130; READ response 46/2/48/110; READ request app 0/pad 0/data 0/frame 74, requested length 46. These numbers are regression expectations, not constants for display. The current exported protocol tree does not separately decode AETH or ICRC. If showing a verified structural byte region, distinguish derived layout from decoded values; otherwise label these as conceptual protocol structure. Never fabricate syndrome, MSN or CRC values. The capture's recorded frame length is not a complete measurement of all physical-link overhead. [R9–R12]

title: One Work Request can produce more than one packet
learnerCopy:
Our actual messages are deliberately short. Each request containing data in this reference run fits in one transport packet. That makes it easy to follow the relationship between one Work Request and the packet we see. It does not mean a Work Request always maps to one packet.

The transport needs to respect a configured path MTU. When a message is larger than the usable transport packet payload, the provider can break the operation into a sequence of packets. In an illustrative SEND with 2,500 application bytes and a 1,024-byte path-MTU payload, the data can be carried in 1,024, 1,024 and 452-byte portions. The transport packet forms are First, Middle and Last. A sufficiently small message uses Only instead. The receiver associates the packets with the same operation and its prepared destination, rather than treating each packet as a new receive WR.

Here is where the TCP example helps. TCP sequence numbers describe positions in a byte stream; RC packet sequence numbers track transport packet sequencing. Do not apply the TCP rule of adding the payload byte count to an RDMA PSN. For a simple multi-packet SEND, successive packets use successive PSNs. ACKs and READ responses have operation-specific sequence semantics, and PSNs wrap in their 24-bit space. We will not generalize the simple SEND pattern to every packet form.

Our small reference runs do not record this larger transfer. The diagram is a conceptual example to explain why the opcode and PSN exist.
visualSpec: Conceptual example labelled continuously: one SEND WR (length 2500) → three packet cards, offsets 0–1023 / 1024–2047 / 2048–2499; PSNs 100, 101, 102 illustrative; First/Middle/Last labels, no invented capture frame numbers or packet hex. **Select each packet** highlights precise source/destination range; one B receive instruction is consumed for the message, one successful receiver completion after full message in this model. **Compare small captured SEND** restores `b:packet:3` actual Only/PSN. Use byte-aligned bars. No fake performance, ACK-per-packet promise or claim that Ethernet MTU equals RDMA path MTU. Primary **Consider reliability and retries**.
revealCopy: A WR describes an application operation; a packet is one transport unit used to carry out that operation. Packet sequence numbers are not the same as byte counts or completion IDs. [R1, R5, R9, R11]

title: Why is a reliable operation possible over UDP?
learnerCopy:
UDP encapsulation does not make a transport reliable by itself. Our QPs use Reliable Connected transport. The RDMA transport tracks packet sequence progress, recognises acknowledgement or negative-acknowledgement information and can retry when appropriate. The provider implements this machinery: software RXE in our lab, representative hardware in an RNIC.

Imagine that one packet of a multi-packet SEND is lost. The receiver cannot treat a later packet as if the missing part of the operation had already arrived. Reliable transport uses its sequence and acknowledgement rules to detect and recover from problems. The exact response, retry and ordering behaviour depends on the transport and implementation. If required progress cannot be made, the application can observe an unsuccessful Work Completion or reach a timeout in its own wait logic.

There is another kind of delay that does not require a congested network: the receiver may have no posted receive work when a SEND arrives. The RNR mechanism tells us that endpoint readiness and network packet delivery are separate issues. An application may also fail to complete because an MR key, address range or permission is invalid.

We should therefore not jump from "a completion did not arrive" to "the switch must be dropping packets." First identify the operation and the evidence available at each layer. In a real AI cluster, congestion and loss are very important, but they are not the only reasons an operation may fail to progress.
visualSpec: Conceptual three-packet SEND from 8.5. **Illustrate missing packet** marks one range missing, shows incomplete logical operation. **Illustrate transport recovery** reveals retry conceptually and completion eligible after required data/transport progress, no exact timing or fabricated NAK format. Separate selectable **Receiver not ready** and **Remote access rejected** cases return to 5.4 and 4.6 concepts, without mixing SEND with RETH access rejection: latter is separate WRITE/READ scenario.
